name: Review
summary: For reviewing other people’s pull requests to Physlib.
description: For reviewing pull requests (proposed changes) to Physlib: checking that definitions match the physics, suggesting better statements or proofs, and helping authors get their work merged.
criteria: The reviews were on pull requests to leanprover-community/physlib and contained substantive comments, not only approvals.
The reviews improved the physics, the Lean code or the documentation of the change.
Links to the reviewed pull requests or review threads are given as evidence.
guidance: One report usually covers several substantive reviews over a period of time, or the careful review of one large change. A single short review is not enough.
examples: Reviewed 10 pull requests on quantum mechanics
Reviewed 25 pull requests on special relativity and the Lorentz group
Reviewed 50 pull requests across Physlib over a year
A detailed review of the pull requests introducing the Higgs potential

name: Maintenance
summary: For keeping Physlib building and up to date.
description: For work that keeps Physlib building and usable: updating it when Lean or Mathlib release new versions, fixing what those updates break, and looking after the automatic build checks (CI), linters, documentation and the issue tracker.
criteria: The work was maintenance of Physlib or its infrastructure, for example version updates, CI, linting, replacing deprecated lemmas, tooling or issue triage.
The work was merged or otherwise adopted by the project.
Links to the relevant pull requests, commits or issues are given as evidence.
guidance: One report usually covers several months of regular maintenance, or one substantial piece of infrastructure work.
examples: Kept Physlib building against new versions of Lean and Mathlib for six months
Replaced deprecated Mathlib lemmas throughout Physlib
Set up and looked after the linters and CI checks
Triaged and closed 40 issues

name: Refactoring
summary: For restructuring existing Physlib code so it is simpler or more general.
description: For changing the structure of existing Physlib code without adding new results: generalising definitions, merging duplicate definitions, reorganising files, or speeding up compilation, so that later work is easier.
criteria: The change restructured existing Physlib code rather than adding new results.
The change was merged and leaves the library easier to use or extend.
Links to the relevant pull requests are given as evidence, with a short account of what changed and why.
guidance: One report usually covers one refactor that touched many files or removed a significant amount of duplication.
examples: Refactored tensors in Physlib to be easier to use
Unified two competing definitions of the Lorentz group
Reorganised the quantum mechanics files into a clear module structure
Generalised the harmonic oscillator from one to n dimensions

name: Foundational Work
summary: For basic definitions that other parts of Physlib build on.
description: For setting up the basic definitions and first properties of an area of physics in Physlib, such as spacetime, tensors, quantum states or thermodynamic systems, so that other results can be stated and proved.
criteria: The work introduced or substantially developed basic definitions and their elementary properties in Physlib.
The work was merged and is used, or is designed to be used, by other parts of the library.
Links to the relevant pull requests and modules are given as evidence.
guidance: One report usually covers the foundations of one area, typically built up over several pull requests.
examples: Built up the foundations of quantum mechanics
Defined spacetime and its basic properties
Set up thermodynamic systems and the laws of thermodynamics
Defined Feynman diagrams and their first properties

name: Formalisation
summary: For adding new lemmas and definitions to Physlib or PhyslibAlpha.
description: For adding to Physlib: stating and proving results from physics, building on the existing definitions, and adding worked examples. This includes many small additions across different areas, as well as one larger result.
criteria: The work added new results, proofs or examples to Physlib, rather than restructuring existing code or setting up the basic definitions of an area.
The work was merged and follows the library’s conventions.
Links to the relevant pull requests are given as evidence.
guidance: One report usually covers several pull requests over a period of time, possibly across different areas, or one substantial result.
examples: Contributed 10 pull requests across electromagnetism, thermodynamics and quantum mechanics
Formalised the Lorentz force law and its first consequences
Added 30 lemmas on the quantum harmonic oscillator
Proved anomaly cancellation for a new family of gauge theories

name: Documentation
summary: For explaining Physlib: docstrings, module overviews, guides and tutorials.
description: For making Physlib easier to understand and use: writing docstrings and module overviews, explaining the physics behind definitions, and writing guides and tutorials for newcomers.
criteria: The work documented Physlib, for example docstrings, module overviews, explanations of the physics, guides or tutorials.
The documentation was merged or published, and is accurate and clear.
Links to the relevant pull requests or published pages are given as evidence.
guidance: One report usually covers documenting one area thoroughly, or one substantial guide or tutorial.
examples: Wrote the documentation for the Lorentz group modules
Added docstrings explaining the physics throughout the quantum mechanics files
Wrote a getting-started tutorial for new Physlib contributors
Documented the conventions used for tensors and index notation

name: Test
summary: For trying out the form, the review and the signing. Not a record of real work.
description: Test submissions go through the same steps as a real submission, from the form to the pull request and the signing, so that the whole process can be tried out. They need no maintainer approval: merging the pull request is enough. Test reports are marked as tests, are not numbered, and are not listed with real reports.
criteria: The submission is clearly a test and does not claim credit for real work.
guidance: The form is filled in with example data, except the GitHub username and ORCID iD. Enter your own GitHub username to send the test.
